stem:
A 12-day-old term boy is brought to a rural emergency department at 3 a.m. by his parents who noticed poor feeding for the previous 24 hours and cool, mottled legs this morning. He was born at term by uncomplicated vaginal delivery, discharged at 24 hours after a normal newborn examination and passed the pre-discharge pulse oximetry screen with post-ductal saturation of 96 percent. He is exclusively breastfed and had been feeding well until yesterday.

On examination he is pale, grunting, and lethargic. The upper limbs are warm and pink; the lower limbs are cool and dusky. Right upper limb blood pressure is 88/48; right lower limb blood pressure is 40/22. There is a soft systolic murmur at the left sternal edge and a hyperdynamic praecordium. Femoral pulses are just palpable and delayed compared with the brachial pulses. Liver edge is palpable 3 cm below the costal margin.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 176, blood pressure 88/48 right arm and 40/22 right leg, respiratory rate 68 with grunting, SpO2 pre-ductal 98 percent and post-ductal 90 percent on room air, temperature 36.4 degrees
data_table.Bedside investigations: capillary blood glucose 3.6 mmol/L (3.5-5.5), venous lactate 5.4 mmol/L (0.5-2.2), chest x-ray with cardiomegaly and pulmonary venous congestion, four-limb blood pressures with a 40 mmHg upper to lower limb gradient
data_table.Post-transfer arrangements: the nearest paediatric intensive care retrieval team has been contacted and estimated time of arrival is 90 minutes

lead_in: In addition to initial resuscitation, what is the single most important pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Administer an intravenous adenosine 100 microgram/kg rapid bolus for suspected supraventricular tachycardia
options.rationale: Sinus tachycardia at 176 with a differential four-limb blood pressure and a chest x-ray consistent with heart failure is not SVT. Adenosine will not correct ductal closure. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 10 nanograms/kg/minute after securing peripheral access
options.rationale: A late-presenting ductal-dependent left-sided lesion such as coarctation or interrupted aortic arch reopens with prostaglandin E1. The infusion is started before intubation or catheter placement in a shocked newborn to restore lower body perfusion. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse

options.text: Commence an intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/minute as first-line vasoactive support
options.rationale: Inotropes increase myocardial oxygen demand in an unrelieved obstruction. Prostaglandin reopening of the duct treats the underlying cause and is the correct first pharmacological step. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse

options.text: Administer an intravenous frusemide 1 mg/kg bolus with fluid restriction for pulmonary venous congestion
options.rationale: Diuresis will worsen an already-hypotensive systemic circulation and does nothing for the closed duct. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse

options.text: Administer an intravenous ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg dose for empirical late-onset neonatal bacterial sepsis
options.rationale: Empirical antibiotics are reasonable adjuncts but do not address the underlying ductal-dependent lesion. Prostaglandin is the single most important pharmacological intervention. (Source: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Neonatal cardiovascular collapse

explanation.summary: The pre and post ductal saturation differential, four-limb blood pressure gradient, hepatomegaly, and lactic acidosis in a 12-day-old point to a critical left-sided ductal-dependent lesion whose duct is closing. Prostaglandin E1 reopens the duct and restores lower body perfusion; it should be started before any other pharmacological intervention while awaiting retrieval. Passing the pulse oximetry screen does not exclude the diagnosis because the post-ductal saturation is initially maintained by the patent duct.
key_points: Prostaglandin E1 at 5 to 10 ng/kg/min reopens the arterial duct in ductal-dependent lesions
Four-limb blood pressures showing an upper to lower gradient over 20 mmHg suggest coarctation or interrupted arch
The pulse oximetry newborn screen picks up right-sided but not all left-sided lesions - late collapse is possible
explanation.pearls: Any collapsed neonate presenting in the second week should have prostaglandin E1 started empirically while echocardiography is arranged. Apnoea is the main dose-related side effect - be prepared to intubate.

sources.label: Australian Newborn Pulse Oximetry Screening Statement

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate versus surgery for tubal ectopic
stem:
A 28-year-old nulligravid woman presents to an early pregnancy assessment service with 3 days of intermittent left iliac fossa pain and light brown vaginal spotting. Her last menstrual period was 6 weeks and 4 days ago and she confirmed pregnancy on a home test 2 weeks ago. She is haemodynamically stable, well perfused, has minimal focal tenderness on abdominal palpation, and is not distressed.

A transvaginal ultrasound today shows an empty uterine cavity with a 12 mm endometrium, an unruptured left tubal mass of 28 mm without embryonic cardiac activity, and no significant free fluid in the pouch of Douglas. Serum beta hCG this morning is 4200 IU/L (48 hour rise ceased). She is a reliable follow-up attendee, has no active liver, renal or haematological disease, and is not breastfeeding. She has a strong preference to avoid surgery if possible.

data_table.Investigations: beta hCG 4200 IU/L, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-165), platelets 240 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 22 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 60 micromol/L (45-90), blood group O rhesus positive
data_table.Imaging: transvaginal ultrasound with empty uterus, left tubal mass 28 mm without cardiac activity, no free fluid

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Proceed to urgent laparoscopic left salpingectomy under general anaesthesia within the next operating theatre list
options.rationale: Surgical management is required for beta hCG at or above 5000 IU/L, ruptured ectopic, haemodynamic instability, or contraindications to methotrexate. None apply here. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Repeat the beta hCG in 48 hours and defer treatment until a further rise or fall is confirmed on trend
options.rationale: The diagnosis of tubal ectopic is already made on ultrasound with a plateaued beta hCG. Deferring treatment for another 48 hours risks rupture. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Administer a single dose intramuscular methotrexate 50 mg/m2 with weekly serum beta hCG surveillance to resolution
options.rationale: RANZCOG allows methotrexate for a tubal ectopic when beta hCG is under 5000 IU/L, the mass is under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity is present, pain is minimal, follow-up is reliable, and there are no medical contraindications. All criteria are met here. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Commence expectant management with weekly clinical and biochemical review until spontaneous resolution occurs
options.rationale: Expectant management is confined to a very low and falling beta hCG (typically under 1500 IU/L and declining). At 4200 IU/L it is not appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

options.text: Administer a course of mifepristone with misoprostol as a medical evacuation of the uterine pregnancy retained
options.rationale: Mifepristone-misoprostol is for intrauterine pregnancy and has no role in tubal ectopic. It does not resolve tubal implantation. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 61 Ectopic Pregnancy

explanation.summary: This unruptured tubal ectopic meets every RANZCOG criterion for medical management: beta hCG under 5000 IU/L, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, and no medical contraindications. Single dose methotrexate 50 mg/m2 IM with weekly hCG surveillance is appropriate. Surgery is reserved for higher hCG, rupture, or failure of methotrexate.
key_points: RANZCOG methotrexate criteria: hCG under 5000, mass under 3.5 cm, no cardiac activity, minimal pain, reliable follow-up, no MTX contraindications
Surgical management indicated if any criterion is unmet or rupture is suspected
Weekly hCG until under 5 IU/L is the AU surveillance protocol
explanation.pearls: The AU hCG surgical cut-off is 5000 IU/L, not 3000. This is a common misremember.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Ectopic pregnancy medical management

stem:
A 32-year-old primigravida at 34 plus 3 weeks gestation is admitted from clinic with a headache and epigastric pain. Her blood pressure recorded three times over 30 minutes is 168/112, 172/108 and 170/110. She has 3+ proteinuria on dipstick and a spot protein to creatinine ratio of 65 mg/mmol (less than 30). She has brisk lower limb reflexes with 4 beats of clonus on the right.

On examination she is uncomfortable but alert. Uterine tone is soft, cardiotocography is normal with a reactive trace, and there are no vaginal loss or contractions. Full blood count shows a platelet count of 135 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), alanine aminotransferase 90 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90) and lactate dehydrogenase 340 U/L (less than 250). Antenatal corticosteroids for lung maturation were given three days ago in another episode of admission.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 96, blood pressure 170/110, respiratory rate 18, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees, foetal heart rate 145
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 118 g/L (115-165), platelets 135 x10 to the 9 per litre (150-400), ALT 90 U/L (less than 35), creatinine 82 micromol/L (45-90), LDH 340 U/L (less than 250), urate 0.42 mmol/L (0.15-0.36)

lead_in: In addition to intravenous antihypertensive therapy, what is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Administer intravenous phenytoin 15 mg/kg loading dose as an alternative to magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is superior to phenytoin for both prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures (MAGPIE and Collaborative Eclampsia trials). Phenytoin is not first-line. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Administer intramuscular betamethasone 11.4 mg as a repeat antenatal corticosteroid dose for lung maturation
options.rationale: Corticosteroids were given three days ago and repeat dosing is not indicated so soon; more importantly, the priority now is seizure prophylaxis and delivery planning, not lung maturation. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Administer intravenous frusemide 40 mg as diuretic therapy for suspected preeclampsia-related pulmonary oedema
options.rationale: There are no clinical or oxygenation findings to suggest pulmonary oedema and diuresis is not part of seizure prophylaxis. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading dose over 20 minutes then 1 g/hour maintenance infusion
options.rationale: Severe preeclampsia with neurological features (headache, hyperreflexia, clonus) meets SOMANZ criteria for magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis. The 4 g load followed by 1 g/hour infusion is the AU standard. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

options.text: Administer intravenous diazepam 10 mg as a prophylactic anticonvulsant while transfer to a tertiary unit is arranged
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines are used for seizures resistant to magnesium sulfate but not as first-line prophylaxis in preeclampsia. (Source: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline)
source_refs: SOMANZ Hypertension in Pregnancy Guideline

explanation.summary: Severe preeclampsia with neurological signs (headache, hyperreflexia, clonus) and biochemical involvement (raised ALT, thrombocytopenia, raised urate) is a SOMANZ indication for magnesium sulfate seizure prophylaxis. The AU regimen is a 4 g load over 20 minutes and a 1 g/hour maintenance infusion. Antihypertensive therapy and planning for delivery run in parallel.
key_points: MgSO4 4 g IV load over 20 min then 1 g/hour infusion; monitor knee reflexes, respiratory rate, and urine output
MgSO4 is superior to phenytoin and diazepam for both prevention and treatment of eclamptic seizures
Severe preeclampsia = severe hypertension plus organ involvement OR neurological features
explanation.pearls: Loss of patellar reflexes is the first sign of magnesium toxicity. Calcium gluconate 1 g IV is the antidote.

subtopic_detail: Anti-D immunoglobulin timing after sensitising event
stem:
A 24-year-old primigravida at 22 weeks gestation presents 6 hours after a minor motor vehicle crash. She was a restrained front seat passenger in a low-speed rear-ending collision, has no abdominal pain, no per vaginal bleeding, no uterine tenderness on palpation and a reassuring cardiotocography trace. Foetal biometry is appropriate for gestation on point-of-care ultrasound with an anterior placenta well clear of the internal os.

Her booking blood group is O rhesus negative with no red cell antibodies detected at 28 week screen (which has not yet been performed at her current gestation). She has previously declined the 28-week prophylactic anti-D dose plan but consents today to being managed as clinically indicated. She is otherwise well and has no other injuries.

data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 122 g/L (115-165), blood group O rhesus negative, indirect antiglobulin test negative, Kleihauer-Betke test pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step regarding anti-D immunoglobulin?

options.text: Await the Kleihauer-Betke test result before deciding whether to administer any anti-D immunoglobulin at all
options.rationale: Anti-D should not be delayed for the Kleihauer-Betke. The initial 625 IU dose is given first; Kleihauer only guides ADDITIONAL doses beyond that. (Source: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: Administer intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin 250 IU now given the minor severity of the mechanism of injury
options.rationale: The 250 IU dose is used before 12 weeks; from 12 weeks onward the AU standard dose is 625 IU regardless of the severity of the sensitising event. (Source: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: Withhold anti-D immunoglobulin because the placenta is anterior and the motor vehicle mechanism is very low grade
options.rationale: Placental location and mechanism grade do not exclude sensitisation risk. Any abdominal trauma after 12 weeks in a rhesus D negative woman is a potentially sensitising event. (Source: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: Administer intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin 1500 IU now as a routine 28 week prophylactic dose in advance
options.rationale: The 1500 IU is the routine 28-week prophylactic dose, not the event-triggered dose. Event doses are 625 IU (from 12 weeks) or 250 IU (under 12 weeks). (Source: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

options.text: Administer intramuscular anti-D immunoglobulin 625 IU now and await Kleihauer-Betke to guide any additional dose
options.rationale: For a potentially sensitising event after 12 weeks in a rhesus D negative woman, NBA recommends 625 IU IM anti-D within 72 hours (ideally as soon as possible). The Kleihauer-Betke test then quantifies foetomaternal haemorrhage to guide additional dosing if required. (Source: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin)
source_refs: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: This woman has had a potentially sensitising event after 12 weeks. NBA guidance is to give 625 IU IM anti-D as soon as possible (and within 72 hours). Kleihauer-Betke testing quantifies foetomaternal haemorrhage and guides any additional doses. The 1500 IU prophylactic 28-week dose is a separate schedule.
key_points: Event doses: 250 IU under 12 weeks; 625 IU from 12 weeks onward; Kleihauer guides additional dosing
Routine 28 and 34 week prophylactic doses are 625 IU each (or a single 1500 IU dose depending on local schedule)
Do not wait for Kleihauer to give the first event dose
explanation.pearls: Every 4 mL of foetal red cells requires an additional 625 IU. Read the Kleihauer as a dose driver, not a gate.

sources.label: NBA Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin
RANZCOG C-Obs 6 Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) Immunoglobulin

stem:
A 32-year-old woman with a body mass index of 26 attends a diabetes in pregnancy clinic at 27 weeks gestation after a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test performed at 26 weeks in her local pathology lab. Her fasting glucose was 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour glucose 9.8 mmol/L, and 2-hour glucose 8.3 mmol/L (fasting less than 5.1, 1-hour less than 10.0, 2-hour less than 8.5). She has no personal history of type 2 diabetes, no polycystic ovary syndrome, and her first pregnancy 3 years ago was uncomplicated with a birth weight of 3300 g.

Her first-trimester screening glucose was normal. Booking bloods showed normal HbA1c at 5.3 percent (under 5.7). She is asymptomatic with no polyuria or polydipsia. Foetal biometry at 27 weeks shows appropriate growth with abdominal circumference on the 60th centile.

data_table.Investigations: OGTT fasting 5.1 mmol/L (less than 5.1), 1-hour 9.8 mmol/L (less than 10.0), 2-hour 8.3 mmol/L (less than 8.5), HbA1c 5.3 percent (less than 5.7)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate diagnostic interpretation and next step?

options.text: Diagnose gestational diabetes based on the fasting value meeting the threshold and commence structured dietary advice and self blood glucose monitoring
options.rationale: ADIPS applies IADPSG cut-offs where meeting or exceeding any one of fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0, or 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L confirms GDM. Her fasting value of 5.1 meets the fasting threshold, so GDM is diagnosed on this single value. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes

options.text: Repeat the oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks because none of the individual values definitively exceeded the diagnostic thresholds today
options.rationale: The fasting value of 5.1 meets the threshold (the criterion is greater than or equal to, not strictly greater than). GDM should be diagnosed and treated now. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes

options.text: Reassure that gestational diabetes is excluded because at least two values are required to meet the diagnostic thresholds under the ADIPS pathway
options.rationale: ADIPS requires only one abnormal value on the 75 g OGTT to diagnose GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes

options.text: Diagnose overt diabetes in pregnancy based on the OGTT results and commence subcutaneous insulin as first-line pharmacotherapy today
options.rationale: Overt diabetes in pregnancy requires fasting glucose at or above 7.0, HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent, or random glucose at or above 11.1. Her values are consistent with GDM, not overt diabetes. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes

options.text: Repeat the HbA1c and treat as gestational diabetes only if the result rises to at least 6.5 percent on the follow-up sample
options.rationale: HbA1c is not used to diagnose or exclude GDM; the OGTT is the diagnostic test. HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent flags overt diabetes, not GDM. (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes)
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes

explanation.summary: The ADIPS diagnostic thresholds for GDM on a 75 g OGTT are fasting at or above 5.1 mmol/L, 1-hour at or above 10.0, and 2-hour at or above 8.5. Any one value meeting or exceeding its threshold confirms the diagnosis. Her fasting value of exactly 5.1 mmol/L therefore meets criteria. Dietary advice and self blood glucose monitoring are first-line.
key_points: ADIPS/IADPSG OGTT thresholds: fasting 5.1, 1-hour 10.0, 2-hour 8.5 mmol/L (any one confirms GDM)
Overt diabetes in pregnancy: fasting at or above 7.0, HbA1c at or above 6.5 percent, random at or above 11.1
First-line management is diet and self-monitoring; escalate to metformin then insulin as needed
explanation.pearls: The trap here is the greater-than-or-equal versus strictly-greater confusion. A fasting exactly on the cut-off IS diagnostic in Australia.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes
RANZCOG C-Obs 7 Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus

subtopic_detail: Postpartum haemorrhage escalation beyond first-line uterotonics
stem:
A 33-year-old multiparous woman has just delivered a live infant weighing 4200 g vaginally after a 60 minute second stage and active management of the third stage with intramuscular oxytocin 10 units. Estimated blood loss at 10 minutes postpartum is 1200 mL from ongoing dark red bleeding per vagina with a boggy fundus at the level of the umbilicus.

Examination under good lighting demonstrates an intact perineum and second-degree perineal tear that has been repaired without ongoing bleeding from the wound. The lower uterine segment is empty on bimanual examination and the placenta was inspected and reported as complete. Bimanual uterine compression and a further intravenous oxytocin 10 unit slow bolus with intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram have been given but the fundus remains soft and bleeding continues at 200 mL per 5 minutes. Blood pressure is 92/58 with pulse rate 122. There is no history of hypertension, coronary disease, or asthma.

data_table.Vital signs: pulse rate 122, blood pressure 92/58, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees
data_table.Investigations: haemoglobin 92 g/L (115-165) on point-of-care testing, thromboelastography pending, blood group known O rhesus positive with active group and hold

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic step?

options.text: Administer repeat intramuscular ergometrine 250 microgram as the second dose within 5 minutes of the first dose given
options.rationale: Ergometrine dose is capped and repeat doses within a short interval risk severe hypertension and coronary spasm. Escalation to a different agent (carboprost or misoprostol) is required. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Administer intramuscular carboprost 250 microgram (repeated every 15 minutes to a maximum of 8 doses) with continuing bimanual compression
options.rationale: For atonic postpartum haemorrhage refractory to oxytocin and ergometrine, the next uterotonic in the RANZCOG PPH cascade is carboprost 250 microgram IM (or into the myometrium), repeated as needed. She has no asthma contraindication. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Commence intravenous magnesium sulfate 4 g loading bolus over 20 minutes for suspected retained postpartum uterine relaxation
options.rationale: Magnesium relaxes uterine muscle and would worsen atony. It has no role in PPH management. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Administer intramuscular oxytocin 10 units as a third dose to overcome the persistent atony via peripheral receptor upregulation
options.rationale: Oxytocin receptors desensitise with repeated dosing during postpartum haemorrhage. A different pharmacological class is required at this stage of the cascade. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH

options.text: Administer intravenous tranexamic acid 1 g slow bolus alone and continue observation of uterine tone without further uterotonics
options.rationale: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is indicated (WOMAN trial) and should be given, but it does not replace ongoing uterotonic escalation for a still-atonic uterus. (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH)
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH

explanation.summary: This is atonic PPH refractory to first-line oxytocin and ergometrine. The next uterotonic in the RANZCOG cascade is carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes (max 8 doses) provided the woman is not asthmatic. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV should be given in parallel per the WOMAN trial and blood products activated. Mechanical measures (bimanual compression, intrauterine balloon) continue throughout.
key_points: PPH uterotonic ladder: oxytocin, ergometrine (contra in HTN/CAD), carboprost (contra in asthma), misoprostol PR
TXA 1 g IV within 3 hours halves death from bleeding (WOMAN trial)
Repeat oxytocin has diminishing return due to receptor desensitisation
explanation.pearls: Ergometrine's contraindication is hypertension and coronary disease; carboprost's is asthma. Read the case for the contraindication that decides between them.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 43 Prevention, Detection and Management of PPH
WOMAN Trial Collaborators. Effect of early tranexamic acid administration on mortality in women with PPH. Lancet 2017
